furosemide-lasix-bumetanide-torsemide.why: Volume overloaded — loop diuretic for rapid symptom improvement.

hydroxyurea.why: Stimulates fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production — improves symptoms long-term.

folic-acid.why: Supports erythropoiesis — standard in sickle cell disease.

prbc-transfusion-exchange-transfusion.why: ACS with hypoxia unresponsive to O2 — transfusion to dilute HbS. Goal HbS <30%.

physical-exam-general-appearance.why: Full pediatric exam for chronic disease.

physical-exam-abdomen.why: Assess for hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive.

sweat-chloride-test.why: Gold standard for CF diagnosis. >60 mEq/L = positive.

sputum-culture.why: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, S. aureus, H. influenzae common in CF.

pancreatic-elastase-stool.why: Assess pancreatic insufficiency — common in CF.

pulmonary-function-tests.why: Obstructive pattern. FEV1 monitoring guides therapy.

fat-soluble-vitamins-adek.why: Supplementation required due to fat malabsorption.

airway-clearance-therapy.why: Chest physiotherapy, PEP valve, vest therapy.

consult-pediatric-pulmonology.why: CF center referral for multidisciplinary care.

cbc-with-differential.why: Assess degree of anemia from blood loss. Platelet count.

physical-exam-chest-lungs.why: A chest and lung exam is essential here because the patient's tachypnea and tachycardia, combined with her vomiting and altered mental status, could point to a serious metabolic acidosis—like diabetic ketoacidosis—where the lungs try to "blow off" acid by breathing deeper and faster. Listen for Kussmaul respirations: deep, rapid, sighing breaths that would confirm the body is trying to correct a low pH. If her lungs are clear, it shifts your focus firmly away from a primary pulmonary cause and onto the metabolic picture.

hemoglobin-a1c-blood__d2__p88b35a42s22__.why: Mr. Uche Emecheta is a middle-aged man with bilateral leg pain on exertion, pulse 102, BP 133/88. This is classic claudication — his legs demand more blood flow during walking than his narrowed arteries can deliver. The pain is a supply-and-demand crisis: working muscle needs oxygen, stenotic vessels can't increase flow, so ischemia forces him to stop. When he rests, demand drops below supply, the pain resolves. Now look at his risk factors — hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidemia, and newly diagnosed diabetes. Diabetes accelerates atherosclerosis through a specific mechanism: chronic hyperglycemia glycates vessel wall proteins, stiffening the endothelium and driving plaque formation in the same medium-sized arteries that supply the legs. So the HbA1c here isn't a screening test — it tells us how aggressively his glucose has been damaging his vessels over the past three months. If his A1c is high, his claudication is driven by a modifiable process we can slow. If it's controlled, we focus harder on smoking cessation and statins. Either way, this number reframes his leg pain from a mechanical problem to a metabolic one.

lipid-profile__d2__p88b35a42s22__teach-m.why: The leg pain on exertion is a demand-ischemia signal — the calf muscles are outrunning their blood supply every time he walks. That supply is choked by atherosclerotic plaques, and lipids are the raw material those plaques are built from. So checking his lipid profile tells us how much new fuel is available to grow more blockages. His LDL drives endothelial deposition, oxidation, and foam cell formation — the whole cascade that tightens the lumen. Treating that LDL below 100, ideally below 70, slows or halts plaque progression. Without it, his walking distance keeps shrinking and the risk of critical limb ischemia climbs. This order is about whether we can stop the pipe from narrowing further.

microalbumin-urine-24-hour-or-spot__d2__.why: He has newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, so his endothelium has been bathed in high glucose for months. That glucose directly damages the glomerular basement membrane, widening the pores and letting albumin slip through. This happens long before his creatinine budges — microalbuminuria is the earliest detectable sign of diabetic nephropathy. We're screening for early disease because catching it now lets us start an ACE inhibitor and slow the progression before protein spills become irreversible. The same microvascular damage that's causing his claudication — smoking plus hyperglycemia — is also attacking his kidneys. If his urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is elevated, we know the vascular injury isn't limited to his legs. What would you expect to see on his foot exam if the microvascular disease is already advanced?

ankle-brachial-index-arterial-doppler-lo.why: The leg pain on exertion is a supply-demand mismatch. Atherosclerotic plaques in the iliac or femoral arteries create a fixed resistance; during walking, the calf muscles demand more oxygen than the narrowed vessel can deliver. The pain is ischemic — the muscle is screaming for blood it cannot get. Rest lowers metabolic demand back below the supply threshold, so the pain resolves. That pattern — reproducible, distance-dependent, rest-relieved — is classic claudication. The ABI measures the pressure drop across the stenosis: a normal ankle pressure equals or exceeds brachial pressure (≥1.0), but a blocked artery drops the distal pressure. A ratio below 0.7 confirms hemodynamically significant disease. We need this number to stage severity and decide whether to pursue revascularization or start medical therapy.

metformin__d2__p32b30a42s85__teach-me-v1.why: This man's legs are screaming with every block he walks — but the pain is a messenger, not the enemy. The real problem is that his arteries are clogged, his muscles are starving for oxygen, and his newly diagnosed diabetes is accelerating that destruction silently. Without it, his claudication will worsen, his ABI will drop, and he may face amputation or bypass. physical-exam-neuro-psych__teach-me-v5.why:
Mr. Babatunde Zubairu is awake now — pulse 102, BP 110/70, SpO₂ 96% — but he was found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate below 12. That triad is the opioid toxidrome, and it means his brainstem was flooded with mu-receptor agonists, suppressing the locus coeruleus and the pre-Bötzinger complex. The neuro exam is the only way to confirm he has fully emerged from that suppression — not just breathing on his own, but tracking, following commands, and protecting his airway without drift.

You need to see that his pupils are equal and reactive again — the miosis should reverse as naloxone clears the receptors. You need to check his mental status every 15 minutes for the next hour, because naloxone has a shorter half-life than most opioids, and he could slip back into respiratory depression before the next dose is due. The exam isn't a checkbox — it is the bedside monitor for re-toxication. If his pupils start to pinch again or his alertness fades, you have your answer before the pulse ox drops.

What specific finding on the neuro exam would tell you he's at risk of re-sedating before his respiratory rate changes?

physical-exam-general-appearance__teach-.why:
Mr. Babatunde Zubairu is here with a pulse of 102, blood pressure 110/70, and a respiratory rate of 20 — but he was found unresponsive. Those vitals tell us his body is compensating, but his brain is not awake. The first step isn't a scan or a lab — it's a **general appearance** exam, because your eyes are the most sensitive diagnostic instrument you have in the first 30 seconds.

This order belongs because the mechanism of unresponsiveness is a **failure of arousal or content** in the brainstem or cortex. You need to know *which* before you can treat *what*. Is he posturing? Are his eyes open but not tracking? Is he breathing in a Cheyne-Stokes pattern that points to a metabolic cause? Each of those physical findings slams the door on entire categories of differential — and the general appearance exam is how you open those doors.

At the bedside, you'll watch his breathing pattern, his posture, and his response to voice or sternal rub within seconds. That single observation — is he localizing, withdrawing, posturing, or flaccid? — will tell you if this is opioid toxidrome (pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression) or a structural lesion (asymmetric posturing, gaze deviation). The order buys you a diagnosis before the first needle goes in. What do you see when you look at him?

physical-exam-neuro-psych__peer.why:
Mr. Babatunde Zubairu is sitting in front of you with a pulse of 102, a blood pressure of 110/70, and an SpO₂ of 96% on room air — but his respiratory rate is down at 20, and he was found unresponsive. You cannot clear a toxidrome with a quick glance at the monitor; you need to see the pupils yourself.

The opioid toxidrome works by depressing the brainstem — specifically the pontine respiratory center and the Edinger-Westphal nucleus that controls pupillary constriction. Pinpoint pupils and a low respiratory rate are the same mechanism, two outputs. But you cannot trust the triage note or the paramedic's handoff; you must confirm the pupils are *actually* 1–2 mm and reactive, because a fixed and dilated pupil would flip your differential to a structural brainstem lesion or anticholinergic poisoning.

So you order a focused neuro exam: check pupil size and reactivity, assess the level of consciousness with the AVPU scale, and look for needle tracks on the arms. That exam is the fastest way to lock in the opioid toxidrome before you reach for naloxone. The bedside change? You go from *suspecting* opioid overdose to *knowing* it, and you titrate naloxone based on how the respiratory drive and pupil size respond — not on a guess.

physical-exam-general-appearance__peer.why:
Mr. Babatunde Zubairu is awake now — pulse 102, BP 110/70, RR 20, SpO₂ 96% — but he was found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression. The general appearance exam is your first look at whether he is *back* or still drifting.

Start from the doorway. Is he sitting up? Slumped? Making eye contact? The opioid toxidrome suppresses the reticular activating system — when you reverse it with naloxone, the brainstem wakes up, but higher cortical function may lag. A patient who tracks you with their eyes is different from one who stares through you.

Look for the physical residue of the overdose: needle tracks in the antecubital fossa or between the toes, track marks on the neck. Those are not just historical — they tell you the injection route, which affects how fast the opioid hit the brain (IV = seconds, IM = minutes). If he has fresh puncture sites, the risk of re-overdose is higher because the drug depot in fat or muscle can re-equilibrate after naloxone wears off.

Also check his pupils now. If they are still 1–2 mm despite naloxone, the opioid is still bound or a longer-acting agent (methadone, fentanyl) is on board. If they are 4–5 mm and reactive, you have effectively reversed him — but that window is short.

The general appearance is not cosmetic. It is your first neurologic exam before you do the formal one. What do you see when you walk in the room?

Now his RR is 20 and SpO₂ 96% — that reversal tells you naloxone re-opened the mu-gate and he’s breathing on his own again. No hypoxia, no hypercapnia on these vitals; the threat was purely opioid-driven.

physical-exam-general-appearance__teach-.why:
Mr. Babatunde Zubairu is awake now — pulse 102, BP 110/70, breathing 20, satting 96% on room air. But he was found unresponsive, and that history forces us to look for the driver that is still underneath.

General appearance is our first read on his **neurologic drive**. The exam begins before we touch him — we watch how he holds himself, whether he tracks movement, whether his face is symmetric. Because the opioid toxidrome that left him on the floor suppresses the brainstem reticular activating system. If that suppression is lifting, we should see him wake, orient, and follow commands. If he is still drowsy, still flat, still not tracking — then the opioid has not cleared, and we are at risk of recurrent respiratory depression.

Connect this to his vitals: a RR of 20 with SpO₂ 96% is reassuring now, but it does not tell us what happens in thirty minutes when naloxone wears off. General appearance — his arousal, his posture, his ability to protect his airway — is the real-time window into whether his brainstem is back online or still suppressed. That will drive whether we observe, re-dose, or move him to ICU.

bag-valve-mask-ventilation-airway-manage.why: BVM forces air past a patent airway — but with pinpoint pupils and RR 20, Mr. Zubairu is already breathing adequately on room air. His SpO₂ of 96% means the problem isn't gas exchange, it's CNS drive. Naloxone, not BVM, is the first move here.

glucose-fingerstick__peer__d0__teach-me-.why: Fingerstick glucose here isn't about diabetes — it's the fastest way to rule out a hypoglycemic coma, which can look identical to opioid overdose (pinpoint pupils, unresponsiveness). With this man's RR already back to 20 and SpO₂ 96%, the priority is excluding a reversible metabolic cause before assuming naloxone failure.

toxicology-screen-urine-serum__peer__d0_.why: Naloxone already reversed the pinpoint pupils and bradypnea, so urine tox is confirmatory, not diagnostic. The real value here is ruling out co-ingestants — APAP and ASA — that don’t have a toxidrome but cause delayed hepatotoxicity or acidosis. His normal lactate and SpO₂ already argue against a significant CO or cyanide load.

physical-exam-abdomen.why:
A newborn with jaundice needs an abdominal exam to check for **hepatosplenomegaly** — which would point toward hemolysis (extramedullary hematopoiesis) or biliary obstruction rather than simple breastfeeding jaundice.

If the liver or spleen is palpable below the costal margin, that changes your differential from a benign feeding issue to something structural or hematologic.

A soft, non-distended abdomen with no palpable masses supports the picture of physiologic or breastfeeding jaundice — where the liver and spleen should feel normal.

total-direct-bilirubin.why: This baby has jaundice appearing after day 3–5, which is classic for **breastfeeding jaundice** — but we must confirm it's **unconjugated** (physiologic/feeding-related) and not **conjugated** (pathologic, like biliary atresia). A **fractionated bilirubin** is the single lab that separates these two universes: unconjugated > conjugated means we manage with feeding support and possibly phototherapy; conjugated > unconjugated means we need an urgent ultrasound and surgical referral. This one lab determines whether we optimize breastfeeding or start a workup for neonatal cholestasis.

direct-coombs-test.why: The Direct Coombs test detects antibodies coating the baby's red blood cells — the hallmark of immune-mediated hemolysis from ABO or Rh incompatibility. In this well-appearing term newborn with jaundice appearing after day 3, we need to distinguish benign breastfeeding jaundice from pathologic hemolysis. A positive Direct Coombs would confirm that maternal antibodies are attacking the baby's cells, driving bilirubin production and requiring phototherapy or IVIG. A negative result helps rule out that mechanism and supports the breastfeeding jaundice pathway.

g6pd-screen.why:
A G6PD deficiency can cause a severe hemolytic crisis triggered by seemingly benign exposures — even routine medications in the nursery or maternal substances in breast milk.

In a well-appearing term newborn, a sudden or prolonged rise in unconjugated bilirubin raises the question of non-immune hemolysis, and G6PD deficiency is the most common cause worldwide.

The screen is not about the jaundice itself — it's about identifying a latent risk so you can prevent future life-threatening hemolytic events.

optimize-breastfeeding-lactation-consult.why: The jaundice appeared after day 3–5, which points to breastfeeding jaundice, not physiologic jaundice. The root cause is inadequate intake → fewer stools → bilirubin gets reabsorbed from the gut back into circulation instead of being excreted. Optimizing breastfeeding breaks that loop — more milk in means more stooling out, which physically flushes bilirubin from the enterohepatic circulation.

phototherapy-if-exceeds-bhutani-threshol.why: Phototherapy is the only intervention that physically converts bilirubin into water-soluble isomers that can be excreted without conjugation — it directly breaks the buildup. In this well-appearing term newborn with breastfeeding jaundice, the risk isn't the jaundice itself but crossing the neurotoxicity threshold. So we're not treating the number — we're preventing bilirubin from accumulating enough to deposit in the basal ganglia. The Bhutani nomogram tells us exactly where that danger zone begins for this baby's gestational age and risk level.

cbc-with-differential-reticulocyte-count.why: A normal hemoglobin rules out hemolytic anemia as the driver of jaundice in this well-appearing newborn. The reticulocyte count tells you if the bone marrow is cranking out new red cells to compensate for destruction — a high count suggests ongoing hemolysis. Together, these labs confirm that this is simple breastfeeding jaundice from enterohepatic circulation, not a pathologic process.

tsh.why:
TSH is relevant here because untreated congenital hypothyroidism slows hepatic bilirubin conjugation and clearance, directly prolonging physiologic jaundice.

A well-appearing, feeding newborn with jaundice past day 5 needs this ruled out — hypothyroidism is a treatable cause that can be missed if you only think of hemolysis or obstruction.

The hint is literal: in this baby, a normal CBC and Coombs with prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia makes TSH the next logical stop.

ck-serum__teach-me-v9.why:
Mr. Gustavo Diaz is tachycardic at 110, breathing 22, with a lactate of 2.3. His muscle cells are under attack from the simvastatin-gemfibrozil combination. Gemfibrozil blocks the glucuronidation pathway that normally clears statins, so simvastatin levels skyrocket. At toxic concentrations, the drug poisons mitochondrial function in skeletal muscle, starving the cells of ATP.

Without energy, the sarcolemma cannot maintain its electrochemical gradient. The membrane fails, and the cell's contents — including creatine kinase — spill into the bloodstream. This is not a test of damage; it is a direct measure of membrane rupture. The higher the CK, the more cells have died.

His proximal weakness, myalgias, and even the tachycardia (from pain and metabolic stress) are all downstream of this same mitochondrial poisoning. CK tells us how far the process has progressed. A level above 10 times the upper limit of normal confirms rhabdomyolysis and guides how aggressively we must hydrate to protect his kidneys.

ck-serum__peer__d0__teach-me-v9.why: Mr. Dias is tachycardic at 110 with a lactate of 2.3 — his muscle breakdown is already stressing his volume and metabolic status. The CK will confirm rhabdomyolysis from the statin-gemfibrozil interaction, which drives the weakness and myalgias he’s feeling. A normal renal panel doesn’t rule out the risk yet — the CK tells you how much myoglobin is poised to hit his kidneys.

ua__teach-me-v9.why:
Mr. Gustavo Dias is tachycardic at 110, mildly tachypneic at 22, and has a lactate of 2.3 — his muscles are breaking down faster than his body can clear the debris. A UA is the fastest way to see if that debris is reaching his kidneys.

Here's the mechanism chain: Simvastatin plus gemfibrozil blocks his glucuronidation pathway, so statin levels skyrocket. High statin concentration poisons mitochondrial respiration in skeletal muscle, causing rhabdomyolysis. The muscle cells lyse and dump myoglobin into the bloodstream — a 17 kDa protein that is filtered by the glomerulus but then precipitates in acidic tubular fluid.

The UA will be dipstick-positive for blood without RBCs on microscopy — that's myoglobin, not hemoglobin. The pH will tell you how close he is to acute tubular necrosis. Pigmented casts on sediment confirm tubular injury.

This man's kidneys are the downstream target of a pharmacologic collision. The UA tells you whether that collision has already caused damage — and whether you need to start aggressive IV fluids and urine alkalinization now, before his creatinine starts climbing.

aggressive-iv-fluids__teach-me-v9.why: Mr. Dias, 58, is sitting in front of you with a pulse of 110, a lactate of 2.3, and muscle pain so profound he can barely stand. His muscle cells are dying — the simvastatin-gemfibrozil combo has poisoned his mitochondria, causing rhabdomyolysis. As those cells lyse, they dump myoglobin, potassium, and phosphate into his bloodstream. Myoglobin is a direct nephrotoxin and it casts in the renal tubules, especially when urine flow is low. His tachycardia and borderline lactate already signal volume depletion — his muscles are sequestering fluid as they swell. So aggressive IV fluids aren't supportive care; they are the only intervention that flushes myoglobin through the nephron before it precipitates and shuts his kidneys down. Push crystalloid to force a urine output of 200–300 mL/hour. You are not just treating hypotension — you are racing to prevent pigment nephropathy.

physical-exam-neuro-psych.why:
A focused neuro exam lets you **quantify the pattern of deficits** — is it truly recent memory first, with relative sparing of remote? That hippocampal gradient is the hallmark of Alzheimer's, not vascular dementia or depression.

You're also **ruling out focal findings** — asymmetric weakness, reflex changes, or a frontal release sign like grasp reflex — which would point to a different pathology like a tumor or stroke.

Finally, the **cognitive screening score** (MMSE or MOCA) gives you a baseline to track progression and decide when to start donepezil or memantine. Memory isn't just a complaint — it's a measurable sign.

tsh-b12-rpr.why: These three tests are your **reversible dementia screen**. Before labeling this as Alzheimer's, you must exclude conditions that can mimic it and are treatable: **hypothyroidism** (TSH), **B12 deficiency** (which causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord and cognitive decline), and **neurosyphilis** (RPR — a forgotten cause of progressive dementia). If any of these are positive, your entire management changes.

cbc-bmp-lfts.why: CBC, BMP, and LFTs are screening labs to rule out metabolic and systemic causes of cognitive decline before you settle on a neurodegenerative diagnosis. A subtle electrolyte disturbance, uremia, or hepatic encephalopathy can mimic dementia. These are quick, cheap tests that could save the patient from being labeled with Alzheimer's if the real problem is a reversible metabolic derangement.

ct-mri-brain.why:
We need to look for the structural footprint of Alzheimer's — specifically, hippocampal and medial temporal lobe atrophy, which is the signature of the tau pathology that starts there.

Seeing this pattern on MRI helps distinguish Alzheimer's from other dementias, like frontotemporal (frontal/temporal pole atrophy) or vascular dementia (infarcts or white matter disease).

It also rules in or out reversible structural causes: a subdural hematoma, a slow-growing frontal tumor, or normal pressure hydrocephalus with ventriculomegaly.

The atrophy you see on imaging is the physical correlate of the memory circuits that have already been lost — it confirms the mechanism is neurodegeneration, not something we can fix with surgery.

caregiver-support-advance-care-planning.why: In this case of progressive Alzheimer's dementia, memory and executive function will inevitably deteriorate to the point where your patient can no longer manage finances, medications, or daily safety. Advance care planning ensures their wishes for future care are documented *while they still have capacity to participate* — this is the only window to capture their authentic preferences. The goal isn't to treat the beta-amyloid, but to protect the person from a crisis decision made by a stranger in the ER.

memantine.why: Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist that reduces excessive glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity — a key driver of neuronal death in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s disease. In this patient, the progressive cognitive decline, apraxia, and visuospatial deficits suggest the disease has advanced beyond the mild stage, where memantine is indicated as an add-on to cholinesterase inhibitors. By blocking pathological overstimulation of NMDA receptors, it helps preserve synaptic function and slows functional decline. This order targets the neurodegenerative cascade itself, not just symptoms.

cholinesterase-inhibitor-donepezil.why: The cholinergic system in the hippocampus is essential for memory formation, and in Alzheimer's, those neurons are dying off. Donepezil boosts the remaining acetylcholine by blocking its breakdown, giving the surviving circuits a better signal-to-noise ratio. It doesn't stop the plaques and tangles, but it can slow symptom progression for months to a year. This is the first-line symptomatic treatment for this patient's mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's dementia.

physical-exam-abdomen.why: The abdomen holds the most common site of fatal internal injury in abuse — solid organ laceration or bowel wall hematoma from blunt force. Palpation for distension, guarding, and tenderness is how you find what the history didn't mention.

physical-exam-full-skin-exam-photographs.why: A full skin exam with photographs does two things here. First, it reveals the *distribution* of the burns — the sharp stocking-glove line on the buttocks tells you this is an immersion injury, not an accidental splash, because the skin submerged in hot water has a clear horizontal border. Second, the photographs create objective, timestamped evidence of the cigarette burns (circular, punched-out lesions) and any injuries in different stages of healing — this documentation is critical for the legal and child protection case, not just the medical one. You're not just looking at burns; you're mapping the mechanism of injury onto the child's body.
physical-exam-full-skin-exam-photographs.orderLabel: Physical Exam: Full skin exam + photographs

head-ct.why: A head CT is mandatory here because abusive head trauma is the leading cause of death in child physical abuse, and it often coexists with burn injuries. The same mechanism that caused these burns — a caregiver losing control — can also produce rotational acceleration-deceleration forces to the brain. You cannot clear the cervical spine or the intracranial space based on a normal neurological exam in an infant or young child with this injury pattern. We are looking for subdural hematomas, cerebral edema, or shear injuries that may be clinically silent initially but are immediately life-threatening.

cbc-coags-bmp.why: For this child, the CBC, coagulogram, and BMP serve three distinct purposes. First, a low platelet count or elevated INR could mimic abuse by causing easy bruising and bleeding — we must rule out a coagulopathy before concluding the injuries are inflicted. Second, the BMP checks renal function and electrolytes, which can be deranged by large burns or dehydration from delayed care. Third, the CBC gives a baseline for anemia if there has been significant blood loss from deep burns or occult trauma.

report-to-cps-mandatory.why: The burn pattern—stocking-glove with sharp demarcation, cigarette marks, and facial burns inconsistent with the child's development—is a signature of non-accidental trauma. The inconsistent history and delayed care are additional red flags that, taken together, legally obligate you to report. This isn't a clinical decision you weigh; it's a statutory duty triggered by reasonable suspicion. Reporting now activates the legal and social safety net before the child goes home to further harm.

admit-for-safety.why:
When the story doesn't match the injury — a toddler with immersion burns and cigarette marks whose parents say they "don't know how it happened" — you cannot send them home. The home is the suspected source of the injury.

Admitting for safety removes the child from that environment while you work up the rest of the picture: skeletal survey, head CT, retinal exam. You're not treating the burns alone — you're stopping the ongoing harm.

ophthalmology-exam.why: The playbook hint tells you: retinal hemorrhages are the sentinel sign of abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome). An ophthalmology exam is the only way to see them directly — they are invisible on any scan. In this child with multiple red flags for non-accidental trauma, you are ruling in or out the most lethal concurrent injury. You can't clear the head without looking in the eyes.

skeletal-survey.why: Skeletal survey is the standard for occult injury detection in suspected non-accidental trauma. You're looking for fractures in different stages of healing — old ones suggest ongoing abuse, not a single event. A healing rib fracture or corner metaphyseal lesion would confirm that the burns are just one episode in a pattern, not the whole story.

ana.why: Order ANA to evaluate for systemic lupus erythematosus, given the classic malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, polyarthritis, and constitutional symptoms. A positive ANA is required for the diagnosis and will guide further serologic workup.

cbc-bmp-ua.why: CBC, BMP, and UA are essential to screen for hematologic and renal involvement in suspected systemic lupus erythematosus. Given this patient's malar rash, polyarthritis, and fever, you are ruling out cytopenias (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and active nephritis (hematuria, proteinuria, elevated creatinine). Abnormal findings in these labs would support the diagnosis and guide urgent management.

complement-c3-c4.why: Order Complement C3/C4 to assess for active lupus nephritis or systemic flare, as low levels indicate classical pathway consumption in SLE. This patient’s malar rash, photosensitivity, polyarthritis, and fever meet clinical criteria for SLE, and complement levels help gauge disease activity and guide treatment urgency. Expect low C3 and C4 if she has active immune complex deposition.

airway-respiratory-support.why: This patient is unresponsive with respiratory depression, and the primary threat is airway compromise and hypoventilation. Ordering airway/respiratory support allows you to secure the airway via intubation if the GCS remains depressed, preventing hypoxia and aspiration. This is the cornerstone of management for isolated benzodiazepine overdose, as supportive care alone is expected to lead to full recovery.

toxicology-screen.why: A toxicology screen is essential here to confirm the presence of benzodiazepines and, more critically, to rule out co-ingestants like opioids or alcohol, which would explain the severe respiratory depression and hypotonia. Isolated benzo overdose rarely causes this degree of CNS depression, so a positive screen for other sedatives would change your management and prognosis. Expect the screen to show benzodiazepines, but you are actively looking for additional toxins to guide airway support and avoid flumazenil.

cbc-bmp-lfts.why: A CBC, BMP, and LFTs are essential to screen for co-ingestants and metabolic derangements that could cause or worsen CNS and respiratory depression. In this unresponsive patient with known benzodiazepine overdose, you must rule out hypoglycemia, electrolyte abnormalities, hepatic encephalopathy, or concurrent infection as alternative or contributing causes. These labs also establish a baseline before any potential flumazenil use, which carries seizure risk in patients with underlying metabolic or hepatic issues. Expect normal results in isolated benzo overdose, but abnormal findings would prompt a broader differential and alter management.

supportive-care-observation.why: Supportive care and observation are the mainstay of management for this patient with benzodiazepine overdose, as isolated ingestions rarely cause death and typically resolve with airway protection and respiratory support alone. You are ruling out co-ingestants (e.g., opioids, alcohol, TCAs) that would require specific interventions, and you expect gradual improvement in mental status and respiratory drive over hours with close monitoring. Avoid flumazenil here, as it can precipitate acute withdrawal seizures in a chronic user or unmask TCA toxicity.

psychiatry-consult.why: A psychiatry consult is essential here because the presentation of unresponsiveness and respiratory depression from a confirmed diazepam overdose suggests a suicide attempt or intentional self-harm. This order allows for a formal risk assessment of the patient's mental state, evaluation for underlying psychiatric conditions like depression or anxiety, and initiation of safety planning or involuntary hold if needed. Ruling out a co-ingestant overdose is critical, but the consult addresses the root cause of the overdose event itself.

fundoscopy.why: Fundoscopy is essential here to confirm the presence of bilateral papilledema, which is the hallmark physical finding in Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension. Given her occipital headache, vertigo, and tendency to fall, you are ruling in elevated intracranial pressure as the cause of her symptoms. A normal fundoscopic exam would argue against IIH and prompt a broader differential for her headache and imbalance.

mri-mrv-brain.why: In this patient with occipital headache, vertigo, and gait instability, an MRI/MRV brain is essential to rule out a structural cause such as a posterior fossa mass or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which can present similarly. The MRV specifically evaluates for venous sinus thrombosis, a critical diagnosis to exclude given her hypertension and headache pattern. A normal study supports the working diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension by confirming no mass lesion or hydrocephalus, allowing you to proceed with lumbar puncture for opening pressure measurement.

lp-opening-pressure.why: This patient’s presentation of chronic headache with transient visual obscurations and bilateral papilledema strongly suggests elevated intracranial pressure. An LP with opening pressure is essential to confirm the diagnosis of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension by documenting a pressure >25 cm H2O, and to rule out other causes by ensuring normal CSF composition.

weight-loss.why: Weight loss is the most important long-term intervention for Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH). This patient's presentation with chronic headache, transient visual obscurations, and papilledema is classic for IIH, and weight reduction directly lowers intracranial pressure. You are ruling in the diagnosis by confirming elevated opening pressure on LP, but weight loss is the cornerstone of treatment to prevent vision loss. Expect that sustained weight loss will improve her symptoms and reduce the need for surgical intervention.

acetazolamide.why: Acetazolamide is indicated here because this patient's presentation—occipital headache, vertigo, and gait instability—raises concern for elevated intracranial pressure, and the drug reduces CSF production as first-line medical therapy for idiopathic intracranial hypertension. You are ruling in IIH by confirming elevated opening pressure on LP and normal neuroimaging, and expect acetazolamide to improve her headache and vestibular symptoms by lowering ICP.

ophthalmology-follow-up.why: This patient has papilledema from suspected Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension, and the ophthalmology follow-up is critical to objectively monitor for progressive optic nerve damage. You need serial visual field testing and optic nerve imaging to detect early vision loss that would warrant urgent surgical intervention. Without this, you cannot determine if medical therapy with acetazolamide is preserving her sight or if she needs a shunt.

urine-porphyrins__teach-me-v9.why: Mr. Fabio Dias is 37.7°C, tachycardic at 114, breathing 23 — his skin is blistering on the hands and forearms where sunlight hit after a weekend of heavy beer drinking. The alcohol overloaded his liver's ability to process porphyrins, so unmetabolized uroporphyrins accumulated in his skin. Porphyrins absorb UV light at exactly 400 nm and then release that energy as reactive oxygen species — they literally turn sunlight into a chemical burn in his own tissue. That's why the blisters and peeling only appear on sun-exposed areas while his trunk stays clear. His tachycardia and mild fever are the systemic response to that phototoxic injury — the skin barrier is broken, so inflammation spills into the bloodstream. Ordering urine porphyrins now will show elevated uroporphyrin and coproporphyrin levels, confirming the mechanism before you start phlebotomy and sun avoidance. Without the urine test, you'd be treating a sunburn that isn't one.

hcv-hiv-iron-studies__peer__d1__teach-me.why: The blisters are phototoxicity from porphyrin buildup — alcohol and iron overload both suppress uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase in the liver. For Mr. Dias, hepatitis C and iron studies will tell us if he has secondary hemochromatosis driving the enzyme block. A normal ferritin + negative HCV means it's purely alcohol-induced and will clear with abstinence.

phlebotomy__peer__d0__teach-me-v9.why: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is inhibited by alcohol — you can't make heme, so photosensitizing porphyrins pile up in the skin. UV light excites them, and the energy release shreds capillary walls and keratinocytes right there. That's why his blistering maps exactly to sun geometry, not a random dermatome.

phlebotomy__peer__d2__teach-me-v9.why: Phlebotomy in this case isn't for iron overload — it's therapeutic for porphyria cutanea tarda. Your patient's tachycardia and mild fever suggest alcohol-induced decompensation: the damaged liver can't conjugate porphyrins, so they accumulate in the skin and react with UV light to blister. Phlebotomy lowers hepatic iron, which inhibits uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase and breaks the cycle. Normal SpO₂ and lactate confirm this isn't a hemolytic crisis — the target is ferritin, not hemoglobin.

sun-protection-avoid-alcohol__peer__d1__.why: **Mr. Dias** (HR 114, temp 37.7) — alcohol acutely suppresses ALAS1 feedback, then the rebound spike floods his hepatocytes with porphyrin precursors. Sunlight excites those porphyrins in his skin → singlet oxygen → blistering. The yellow shirt and bottles aren't sentimental — they're the substrate and catalyst.

stabilize-the-patient-ensure-airway-brea.why:
Before a single stitch or dose of antibiotics, you have to answer one question: is this patient about to die from something other than the bite?

The airway, breathing, and circulation you're checking is the same ABC sequence that applies to every trauma — but here, the threat is hidden. The bite itself can lacerate an artery (especially on the face, neck, or hand), cause a tension pneumothorax if the chest wall is punctured, or trigger anaphylaxis from venomous saliva. You can't treat the wound until you know the patient won't arrest from the injury's mechanical consequences.

So the order is mechanical, not pharmacological. You're literally ruling out the three ways the bite could kill before you address the wound. Once ABCs are secure, the patient is physiologically stable enough to tolerate wound exploration, irrigation, and tetanus prophylaxis — all of which cause pain and vagal stress. If you start cleaning a face laceration and the patient's airway is compromised from a hematoma, you've made things worse.

What would you look for to know the airway is truly safe in a patient with a neck bite?
stabilize-the-patient-ensure-airway-brea.orderLabel: Stabilize the patient: ensure airway, breathing, and circulatory status

stabilize-the-patient-ensure-airway-brea.why:
"Stabilize" isn't a checkbox — it's a physics-first reset.

The bite has already broken skin and delivered bacteria deep into tissue. But before we worry about *which* bacteria, we need to know if the patient is perfusing well enough to mount an immune response at all. That's the ABC logic: airway, breathing, circulation. If the patient is hypotensive from blood loss or in respiratory distress from anaphylaxis, the wound is irrelevant — the body can't fight infection without oxygen delivery.

So the order says: pause the wound inspection. Assess the machine first. Is the airway patent? Are breath sounds equal? Is there a pulse? This isn't just protocol — it's the hierarchy of what kills fastest. A compromised airway kills in minutes. Infection kills in hours.

Once ABCs are confirmed stable, *then* you can shift focus to the bite — irrigation, debridement, antibiotics. But without this initial stabilization, you're treating a local problem in a patient whose systemic engine is failing. That's why this order belongs first: it buys you the time to think.
stabilize-the-patient-ensure-airway-brea.orderLabel: Stabilize the patient: ensure airway, breathing, and circulatory status

administer-tetanus-prophylaxis-if-needed.why:
The tetanus bacterium, *Clostridium tetani*, lives in soil and animal saliva. An animal bite drives those spores deep into devitalized tissue — the puncture wound creates a low-oxygen environment. Spores germinate, produce tetanospasmin toxin, and that toxin travels up motor nerves to block inhibitory signaling. The result: uncontrollable muscle rigidity and spasm.

This order belongs because the wound is a direct inoculation event. The bite itself is the mechanism — we're not treating the wound's surface, we're preventing germination inside it. Tetanus prophylaxis isn't about the bite's size or appearance; it's about the anaerobic pocket created by the puncture. If the patient's vaccination status is uncertain or >5 years since last dose, we give Tdap or Td and tetanus immune globulin for dirty wounds like this.

The bedside change: you don't wait for trismus or opisthotonos. You stop the toxin before it reaches the spinal cord. One dose of prophylaxis now prevents a week in the ICU.

obtain-a-complete-blood-count-cbc-and-se.why:
This isn't a routine lab draw — it's a **triage signal** for two distinct emergencies hiding behind a bite wound.

First, the **CBC**: a bite is a **direct inoculation** of oral flora into vascular tissue. If the neutrophil count is climbing, that tells you the immune system has already lost the local fight — bacteria are replicating faster than tissue macrophages can clear them. A rising white count doesn't diagnose infection; it diagnoses **systemic inflammatory response**, which changes your management from "clean and observe" to **IV antibiotics and possible operative washout**.

Second, the **serum glucose**: here's the mechanism most people miss. Rabies virus has a **predilection for the limbic system and autonomic centers**. One of its earliest systemic effects is **dysautonomia** — erratic catecholamine surges that drive glucose up before any neurologic symptom appears. A random hyperglycemia in a bite patient with no diabetes history is a **red flag for CNS involvement** long before they develop hydrophobia or agitation.

At the bedside, these two numbers tell you: *are we still managing a local wound, or has this become a systemic emergency?* The CBC answers "infection," the glucose answers "neuroinvasion." Together, they force a decision point — discharge with wound care, or admit for escalation.
obtain-a-complete-blood-count-cbc-and-se.orderLabel: Obtain a complete blood count (CBC) and serum glucose level

culture-and-debridement-of-the-wound-if-.why:
Let’s talk about why culture and debridement is the first move here, not an afterthought.

A dog or cat bite isn’t a clean puncture. It’s a crush-and-tear mechanism. The tooth drives oral flora — *Pasteurella*, *Staphylococcus*, anaerobes — deep into tissue that’s already devitalized by pressure. Debridement removes that dead tissue, which is essentially bacterial fertilizer. Without it, antibiotics alone can’t penetrate the biofilm that forms in the wound’s anaerobic pockets.

Culturing isn’t reflex. It’s targeted. You culture because empiric coverage fails in about 30% of deep bite wounds — especially if the patient presents late, has diabetes, or the bite is over a joint or tendon sheath. The culture tells you which organism survived your initial amoxicillin-clavulanate, so you can pivot precisely.

At the bedside: debridement and culture turn a blind, infected cavity into a clean, visible wound that can heal. Without them, you’re treating a black box. With them, you own the microbiology and the tissue health.
culture-and-debridement-of-the-wound-if-.orderLabel: Culture and debridement of the wound if appropriate

consult-infectious-disease-specialist-fo.why:
The rabies virus is a bullet — once it enters a peripheral nerve, it travels up the axon at roughly 12–24 mm per day, hidden from the immune system the entire way. By the time symptoms appear, it has already reached the central nervous system, where it is nearly 100% fatal. There is no treatment for established rabies. There is only prophylaxis before the virus crosses into the brain.

That's why this consult isn't about treating an infection — it's about outrunning a timer. The Infectious Disease specialist determines three things: whether the animal's risk profile warrants post-exposure prophylaxis, whether the bite's location (face, hand, or neck) shortens the window because of denser nerve supply, and whether the patient's immunization history is reliable. Each variable shifts the risk-to-benefit calculus.

At the bedside, the decision changes everything. An unvaccinated patient with a bat bite in the neck gets rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated *into the wound itself* and a four-dose vaccine series over 14 days. A fully vaccinated patient with a dog bite on the leg may need only a booster. The specialist maps the virus's potential path against the clock — and that map determines whether the patient leaves the ED with a shot schedule or with a watch-and-wait plan that carries a different kind of weight.
consult-infectious-disease-specialist-fo.orderLabel: Consult Infectious Disease specialist for potential rabies prophylaxis

oxygen__teach-me-v3.why:
Let’s start with what the bite actually does to the body—not the wound itself, but the *whole-body response*.

A large animal bite—especially a crush or puncture from a dog or large cat—triggers a massive sympathetic surge. Pain, fear, and tissue destruction dump catecholamines. That drives tachypnea and a shallow, inefficient breathing pattern. The patient is working hard to move air, but they’re not moving it well.

Now add the mechanism of injury: a bite to the face, neck, or chest can cause direct airway compromise—swelling, hematoma, or even tracheal deviation. But even a limb bite can drop oxygen saturation if the patient is hyperventilating from pain and mismatch.

Oxygen here isn’t about fixing a lung problem. It’s about buying time. You raise the FiO₂ to widen the margin before desaturation hits. While you’re irrigating, assessing nerve and vessel integrity, and deciding on antibiotics, the patient’s oxygen reserve is your safety buffer.

At the bedside: you place the nasal cannula or non-rebreather, and you watch the respiratory rate drop. That’s the catecholamine storm settling because the brain senses it doesn’t have to panic-breathe anymore. The pulse oximeter stays above 97%, and you can focus on the wound without the patient crashing from exhaustion.

So the order belongs because the bite isn’t just a local injury—it’s a systemic stressor that steals oxygen reserve. Oxygen restores that reserve before you need it.

genitalia_exam.why: In a young woman with lower abdominal pain, a genital exam is essential to evaluate for pelvic causes such as ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy, or pelvic inflammatory disease. This exam can reveal cervical motion tenderness, adnexal masses, or discharge that would not be detected on an abdominal exam alone. Ruling out these gynecologic emergencies is critical before attributing the pain to a gastrointestinal source.

physical-exam-general-appearance__d2__te.why: Tom Hayes, 45, pulse 90, BP 101/64, SpO₂ 93% — a man whose GABA receptors have been chronically suppressed by a liter of whiskey daily. When alcohol disappears, those receptors become underactive. The brain loses its main braking system. So the sympathetic nervous system runs unchecked — that's the tremor, the diaphoresis, the hallucinations. General appearance tells you how far this has progressed: is he just tremulous, or is he agitated, confused, unable to track? The difference between mild withdrawal and impending delirium tremens is a clinical gestalt that no lab can capture. You're looking for the point where autonomic overdrive turns into global CNS dysregulation — that's the moment you need ICU-level sedation, not just a benzodiazepine taper. His prior DTs mean his brain has already kindled this pathway; it will escalate faster this time. So your first look across the bed tells you how aggressive your initial CIWA and benzodiazepine strategy needs to be.

physical-exam-general-appearance__d3__te.why:
Tom Hayes — 45, pulse 90, BP 101/64, SpO₂ 93%, seeing bugs on the wall 36 hours out from his last drink — his autonomic nervous system is running without brakes.

That's because ethanol is a GABA-A potentiator and an NMDA antagonist. When he drinks a liter of whiskey daily, his brain compensates by downregulating GABA receptors and upregulating NMDA receptors to maintain baseline function. The moment alcohol leaves his system, the brakes disappear — GABA inhibition collapses while glutamate excitation surges unchecked. So his heart races, he sweats, his hands shake, and his visual cortex starts generating bugs that aren't there. The low-normal BP and borderline SpO₂ tell you he's still compensating, but the tremor and hallucinations say the hyperadrenergic storm is building.

The general appearance exam is your first severity gauge — is he calm enough to interview, or is he crawling out of bed? That single observation tells you whether this is mild withdrawal or the opening act of delirium tremens, which killed him once before. Everything else — CIWA, benzodiazepine dosing, ICU level — follows from that first look.

physical-exam-neuro-psych__d3__teach-me-.why:
This is autonomic and cortical hyperexcitability, not a primary psychiatric break. You stopped the GABAergic brake that was compensating for chronic alcohol-driven NMDA receptor upregulation. Now the excitatory system is unopposed — and it's expressing everywhere. The tremor is spinal motor neuron disinhibition. The hallucinations are temporal lobe irritability. The diaphoresis is sympathetic overflow because the locus coeruleus is also disinhibited.

You don't need imaging to know this is withdrawal. You need to confirm that the exam is symmetrical and the mental status is consistent with a toxic-metabolic delirium — no focal deficits, no papilledema. A normal neuro exam in this context *is* the diagnosis: the mechanism is diffuse, not structural.

What will you start first — the benzodiazepine or the CIWA scoring?

physical-exam-heart-cardiovascular__d3__.why: The heart exam here isn't about ischemia or valve disease — it's the only window into autonomic tone you can lay hands on. Alcohol withdrawal strips GABA-mediated inhibition, so the locus coeruleus fires unchecked, dumping norepinephrine into the circulation. The pulse you feel isn't just fast; it's the sympathetic nervous system screaming without its brake. A hyperdynamic precordium, a flow murmur, a bounding pulse — those are all the same catecholamine surge you see in the tremor and the sweat. If you find a normal, quiet heart in this setting, you need to ask why the autonomic response is blunted — that's how you catch a concurrent infection, a silent MI, or impending cardiovascular collapse before it happens. The stethoscope is your catecholamine meter.

supportive-care-observation__d3__teach-m.why: This patient's brain has been adapting to constant GABA potentiation from alcohol. When the alcohol leaves, the GABA brake releases and NMDA glutamate receptors ramp up unchecked — that's the tremor, the autonomic storm, the hallucinations. Supportive care is the foundation because the brain needs time to rebalance its own inhibitory tone without pharmacologic interference. Benzodiazepines are the rescue tool for severe symptoms, but observation with quiet environment, reorientation, and safety monitoring prevents the spiral into full delirium tremens. The prior DTs tell us his kindling threshold is low — each withdrawal episode makes the next one more explosive. So you watch, you protect the airway, you give thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke's, and you don't reach for flumazenil because that strips away the only GABA tone he has left and guarantees seizures. What CIWA-Ar threshold would prompt you to start benzodiazepines in this patient given his DTs history?
